sections.Astrophysical Alerts:
#### EP261122b: refined X-ray spectrum and optical limits strengthen the high-redshift-GRB hypothesis

Einstein Probe’s refined analysis, reported **24 November 2026 at 12:50:59 UTC**, moves the onset of this fast X-ray transient to **22 November at 08:59:04 UTC**. WXT recorded a single pulse lasting about **120 s**. With Galactic hydrogen column fixed at **3.0 × 10²⁰ cm⁻²**, an absorbed power law gives photon index **1.61 (+0.40/−0.44)** and unabsorbed **0.5–4 keV flux 6.1 (+2.1/−1.4) × 10⁻¹⁰ erg s⁻¹ cm⁻²**. [GCN 46356](https://gcn.nasa.gov/circulars/46356).

FXT began its autonomous exposure at **09:05:03 UTC**, about six minutes after the refined onset, and localized an uncatalogued source to **RA 17.8019°, Dec +1.8008°** (J2000), with a **10 arcsec radius at 90% confidence**, including statistical and systematic uncertainty. Its average 0.5–10 keV spectrum is much softer: photon index **2.99 ± 0.16** and unabsorbed flux **1.20 (+0.08/−0.07) × 10⁻¹² erg s⁻¹ cm⁻²** under the same fixed column. The Circular states that the quoted spectral uncertainties are 1σ.

AZT-33IK R-band imaging, reported **24 November at 23:21:54 UTC**, did not recover the earlier z-band optical candidate, giving **3σ Vega limits R > 21.2** at a midpoint **3.62 h** after onset and **R > 21.3** at **30.06 h**. [GCN 46361](https://gcn.nasa.gov/circulars/46361). The authors’ inference **z ≳ 5** is conditional on EP261122b being a GRB and on a power-law optical decay before the z-band detection; it is not a spectroscopic redshift or confidence limit. The R-band non-detections are compatible with a high-redshift dropout, but dust extinction and light-curve structure remain alternatives.

#### GRB 261121A: IPN triangulation reduces the short-burst search region to 6.2 square degrees

The bright burst was detected by Fermi/GBM, GECAM-B and Konus-Wind on **21 November 2026 at about 13:23:56.5 UTC**. A joint Konus-Wind/Fermi analysis reported on **24 November at 15:25:05 UTC** triangulates it to an annulus centered at **RA 251.829°, Dec −20.132°**, with radius **36.194° ± 0.089° at 3σ**. Intersecting this annulus with the final GBM probability region yields a **6.2 deg² 3σ region**, highly elongated: about **38.4°** long and **12 arcmin** wide. The Sun was approximately **39°** away. [GCN 46357](https://gcn.nasa.gov/circulars/46357).

This materially improves the broad GBM-only localization for counterpart searches, although the IPN team notes that the region may improve further. Localization alone does not identify a counterpart, compact-binary progenitor or gravitational-wave association; follow-up limits must also account for the unusually long, narrow geometry.

#### IceCube-261123A: MASTER reports optical limits for the Bronze track candidate

IceCube detected this track-like event on **23 November 2026 at 06:54:16.99 UTC**. The revised Bronze notice gives an energy estimator of **145.04 TeV**, signalness **0.45677**, atmospheric-background false-alarm rate **1.2048 yr⁻¹**, and direction **RA 320.45°, Dec +24.58°**, with asymmetric 90% PSF-containment uncertainties of roughly 1.4°–1.7°. These quantities make it a candidate, not a confirmed astrophysical neutrino or source association. [IceCube notice](https://gcn.gsfc.nasa.gov/notices_amon_g_b/143530_34667334.amon); [GCN 46345](https://gcn.nasa.gov/circulars/46345).

A MASTER follow-up reported on **24 November at 16:00:35 UTC**. MASTER-Tunka began at **23 November 10:30:44 UTC**, about **3.61 h after the neutrino**, reaching clear-band limits up to about **19.0 mag**; additional Tunka observations followed around 27.8 h, and MASTER-Tavrida observed from **24 November 15:47:56 UTC**, about 32.9 h after the event, reaching up to **17.1 mag**. [GCN 46358](https://gcn.nasa.gov/circulars/46358). The report provides pointing-by-point upper limits and claims no optical transient association. These observations cover finite fields and depths; they do not establish that the neutrino region contained no electromagnetic counterpart.

#### GRB 261119A: Fermi confirms a 0.4-second prompt episode and resolves its spectral ambiguity

Fermi/GBM detected this event on **19 November 2026 at 19:01:35.03 UTC**; SVOM later recovered it offline and provided a much smaller ECLAIRs position. The delayed GBM spectral report was issued **24 November at 21:56:49 UTC**. In 50–300 keV, **T₉₀ ≈ 0.4 s**. Over T₀−0.07 to T₀+0.07 s, a cutoff power law gives the reported index **0.12 ± 0.01** and **E_peak = 118 ± 6 keV**. The **10–1000 keV fluence is (7.4 ± 0.9) × 10⁻⁸ erg cm⁻²**, and the 64 ms peak flux is **11 ± 1 photons cm⁻² s⁻¹**. [GCN 46360](https://gcn.nasa.gov/circulars/46360).

A Band function fits equally well, with **E_peak = 107 ± 3 keV**, **α = 0.30 ± 0.05** and **β = −2.6 ± 0.2**. The competing fits and preliminary status matter: these are not a unique physical spectrum, and the report does not provide a redshift, energetics, counterpart or progenitor classification. The burst was **88° from the LAT boresight**, limiting the relevance of contemporaneous LAT coverage.

#### GRB 261121B: SVOM/GRM measures a multi-pulse, long-duration burst

Fermi/GBM triggered on a likely long burst on **21 November 2026 at 20:27:50 UTC**, localizing it to **RA 255.4°, Dec −60.2°** with **6.0° statistical uncertainty**. [GCN 46328](https://gcn.nasa.gov/circulars/46328). An SVOM/GRM ground analysis reported **25 November at 06:24:30 UTC**, using **20:28:10.500 UTC** as its spectral reference time. GRM finds multiple pulses and **T₉₀ = 37 ± 9 s** in **15–5000 keV**. [GCN 46362](https://gcn.nasa.gov/circulars/46362).

From five seconds before to 35 seconds after the GRM reference time, a power law gives index **−1.60 (+0.12/−0.13)** and **10–1000 keV fluence (4.31 ± 0.98) × 10⁻⁶ erg cm⁻²**. The source was about **83° from SVOM’s optical axis**, outside ECLAIRs’ field of view. The duration and multipulse structure support the operational long-GRB classification, while the report supplies no counterpart, redshift or physical progenitor determination.

#### PKS 2232−488: Fermi-LAT records its brightest daily gamma-ray state

Fermi-LAT reported on **24 November 2026 at 20:09 UTC** that the flat-spectrum radio quasar **PKS 2232−488** (4FGL J2235.3−4836; **z = 0.50581 ± 0.00015**) was strongly active on **23 November**. The preliminary one-day flux above 100 MeV was **(0.3 ± 0.1) × 10⁻⁶ photons cm⁻² s⁻¹**, with statistical uncertainty only: more than ten times the 4FGL-DR4 average and the highest LAT daily flux yet reported for this source. The fitted photon index was **1.8 ± 0.2**, compared with the catalogue value **2.45 ± 0.04**. [ATel 18167](https://www.astronomerstelegram.org/?read=18167).

LAT associated one **10 GeV** photon detected at **12:51:01 UTC** with the quasar at probability **>0.999**. That is a photon–source association probability, not a trials-corrected global significance for the flare. No contemporaneous neutrino association, multiwavelength counterpart change or causal interpretation was reported.
